title: Say My Name: A Conversation About Mentalization
subtitle: This conversation dates back to 2020, in the midst of the pandemic we'd rather forget.
body_html:
Owen Muir, MD, and Michelle Bernabe, RN, talked about what “mentalization” actually is, why safety plans are bullsh*t, and what Destiny’s Child has to do with psychiatry.

This conversation took place in May 2020, during the pandemic, at Brooklyn Minds—the company that came before what is now Radial, at much larger scale.

It’s a Saturday. Michelle Bernabe is a registered nurse at Brooklyn Minds, and we’ve been working hard. I’ve been waking up at 3 am. A psychic would tell you that’s when the ghosts are out—the ancestors. Michelle didn’t know that a psychic and a ghost communicator were in the same line of work.

I told her it’s like being “med-peds.” Or multi-classing in Dungeons & Dragons, such as the Cleric-Thief.

We sat down to talk about this thing we do in therapy to augment Brain Medicine—mentalization-based treatment—and what came out was something I think is worth sharing.

Here is a book I wrote about the modality (Amazon affiliate link).

Owen: So this Brooklyn Minds thing. This MBT thing. It seems like the linchpin.

Michelle: Mentalization-based therapy?

Owen: Treatment, actually. It’s even in the writing— “treatment.” That’s officially what’s on the manual cover.

Michelle: Google seems to validate both.

Owen: It’s the kind of thing I can totally see them doing—the people who created MBT. They clearly, to some degree, really wish they’d named things differently. And even the things they were consistent about, they’re unhappy with.

I heard Peter Fonagy—the MBT creator—and Peter Fugel at the 4th Annual International MBT Conference, and Fugel said, “What’s up with pretend mode? That seems like a terrible name.” And Fonagy said, “Yes, it’s a terrible name. Anthony and I were in a cabin over the weekend coming up with it, perhaps having a drink or something, and now we’ve been using it for ten years. Kind of stuck with it.”

It’s a terrible name. And I think that’s probably true for a lot of things in MBT, which is both a bug and a feature.

Michelle: So define it. Mentalization.

Owen: I mean—it’s like this creature that I know is helpful, maybe like a superhero, but I never can quite see it clearly, so I don’t really know what it looks like.

Michelle: It’s like trying to explain air to someone who knows nothing about chemistry or physics. And then saying it’s really important.

Owen: And people are like, what are you talking about?

Michelle: What are you talking about, and why does this matter?

Owen: So I’ve actually started using examples of how it’s not working. Because that’s a little easier.

Say My Name

Owen: I use Destiny’s Child’s “Say My Name” to illustrate psychic equivalence—feelings equaling facts—and teleological mode, which I call “prove it mode.”

Michelle: Let’s rewind to “Say My Name.”

Owen: So, most of R&B is mentalization failures.

“Every other day, you would call and say, ‘Baby, how’s your day?’ But today it ain’t the same. There’s some mistrust there. Every other word is ‘mm-hmm, yeah, okay.” Could it be that you were in the crib with another lady?”

Michelle: Oh, she knows.

Owen: Facts? Or she’s sure? Or she needs proof to prove her wrong. “Say my name—if no one’s around you, say baby, I love you.” It’s both the psychic equivalence and the prove-it mode. She’s assumed her feelings are the facts. And the only way he can prove it to her is by doing something demonstrative—saying her name—so the other person in the apartment she’s assuming he’s with doesn’t know she exists.

Of course, he could just be, you know, cheating. And told the girl about her. So, there’s not enough information. The whole song is that.

Michelle: What that makes clear to me is this idea of psychic equivalence. I feel it in that song in a way I wasn’t aware of before. Maybe whoever the object of the song is—maybe he’s at a library and can’t say her name. Maybe he’s distracted in some way. And she goes immediately to: you’re cheating on me.

Owen: She might not be wrong. But she might not be right, either.

Real Talk

Owen: R. Kelly has a song called “Real Talk,” which is his side of a phone conversation—an argument with his girlfriend.

Michelle: We’re beyond cancel culture.

Owen: He’s a despicable person. Thus, perhaps because he’s so antisocial—he’s a literal convicted sex criminal, his music does a good job of how to misuse mentalizing. This song starts:

“Hey girl, hey, calm down.”

I’ve never heard “calm down” ever calm anyone down. That alone is a mentalization failure. Does “calm down” work? No. Then why would you ever say it? You wouldn’t—unless your feeling that it would work is the fact that it will work. Which explains why people use this completely ineffective mechanism all the time.

The whole song is either her justifiable paranoia—he’s busted—or it’s psychic equivalence on her part. And he may or may not be misusing mentalizing by trying to lie to her.

Michelle: What do you have to do to lie successfully?

Owen: You have to imagine something about what the other person might believe. Good liars can figure out what you’re gonna buy and what you’re not. So you’re holding the other person’s mind in mind.

Michelle: So a good liar is mentalizing?

Owen: A good liar is essentially pseudo-mentalizing. Because when you’re really mentalizing, it’s for both of us. It’s mindfulness for both of us. There is a way where, in lying, you’re imagining the other person well enough to feed them something they’ll believe. But you’re probably not feeling a lot of empathy, or even imagining why you’re in this position again. So it’s all other, not a lot of self.

If you’re truly mentalizing—really mentalizing—and you’re about to lie to somebody, generally you feel guilty. And you can’t do it.

Try punching someone in the face whom you feel deep empathy for.

Michelle: You can’t.

Owen: So truly mentalizing—being mindful for both of us, imagining what might be in our minds—is actually an inhibitory state against violence and deception. Thus, inaccessable, in many ways, to convicted offender Robert Kelly.

The Safety Plan Problem

Owen: Pretend mode is really important for therapists to understand. It’s fundamentally a disconnect between thought and feeling. When we’re doing safety planning in the ER—you’ve done that before, right?

Michelle: Of course.

Owen: Did you use the safety plan?

Michelle: Heck, no.

Owen: Did you think they cared?

Michelle: No.

Owen: Did they think they were gonna use the safety plan?

Michelle: No.

Owen: Did they do it anyway?

Michelle: Yes.

Owen: Did they think you cared?

Michelle: No.

Owen: So you’re both pretending that this is important, that they’ll use it, enough to go through the exercise.

Michelle: Healthcare in the United States, ladies and gentlemen.

Owen: And importantly—sitting there with a helping professional who’s there, and you’re agreeing to lie to each other. What does that do to trust?

Michelle: Blows it up.

Owen: So by doing this thing that’s supposed to keep people safe, but is phony, we are telling someone: this phony thing is more important than talking about what will actually matter. And I’m going to pretend to believe you when you say you’re going to use these skills. And you’re gonna pretend that I believe what you’re saying. And we’re just gonna pretend at each other so you can get out of here and I can get on with my night. And you can get on with—whatever you’re gonna do.

Michelle: Or I’ll see you here next week.

Owen: The revolving door is one of mistrust. It’s the same thing. Come back and go, “Hey, we’re gonna have that same conversation we had about how I really need to use my coping skills.” And I’m gonna nod and say, “Yep, those coping skills are great.”

So What Would Actually Work?

Michelle: What would a mentalized safety plan actually look like?

Owen: One that doesn’t involve any bullshitting of each other.

Michelle: Well, first, it would entail an authentic and genuine connection.

Owen: Actually be curious about what the other person thinks or feels. And be that way about yourself.

Michelle: When you say it that way— “actually be curious about what the other person thinks and feels”—it’s like, duh. That’s so easy.

Owen: And yet we’re trained not to do it.

Michelle: But then why did I spend seven years in the psych ER not ever seeing that?

Owen: Did you learn something about how it goes when you don’t see it?

Michelle: Yeah.

Owen: Did you learn something about how it goes when you do see it?

Michelle: Yes.

Owen: Then that’s why you spent seven years. Why are lies we both agree to believe part of the fabric of humanity?

Michelle: It’s adaptive.

Owen: How are you doing? Good. Done. We didn’t have to have any conversation about any deeply painful thing. We just passed each other on the street. We’re constantly going through the motions to get through the day, but to deeply, genuinely be curious about every single person’s inner life? It would be exhausting. You’d never get anything done.

So it’s not that mentalizing is good, period. It’s the ability to control—to some degree—when mentalizing is on or offline, that’s tremendously helpful. Sometimes we need to switch it on when our emotions wouldn’t normally. And sometimes we need to switch it off to get ourselves to safety or just not waste our time.

Curiosity Frees Us

Michelle: So how would you work in a broken system more successfully?

Owen: Curiosity. These moments of genuine curiosity, trust, and authenticity. Understanding. Trying to understand. And recognizing when you didn’t—that’s the real one.

Michelle: Recognizing when you didn’t get it?

Owen: Yes! Or, telling a joke that someone actually finds funny. Because you’ve imagined what they’d laugh at and you’re not going to offend them. “Oh, you did a good job of getting me,”—and that thing you said wasn’t expected, but it was palatable to me.

Michelle: Humor.

Owen: Humor is inherently mentalized if it’s funny. Off-color humor is missing the mark. It’s not mentalizing the person. And the response is offense, because you misunderstood me.

And the flip side: I said something sarcastic to you earlier, and you knew it was sarcasm.

Michelle: Because I know you’re a good person, and I know that must have been sarcastic.

Owen: So you’ve mentalized that joke. I actually meant the opposite of what I said. And it’s mentalizing that lets us work out that something offhanded—one sentence which is the opposite of the truth—is in fact meant to underline the point. You felt me on that, not as an insult, but with respect. Because you trust me.

And this is why reincorporation—callbacks—work in comedy. “Oh, that’s the thing you set up twenty minutes ago!” We both understand why the callback is funny, because we shared that experience. That’s mentalizing.

The Chuckles Safety Plan

Owen: Look, I know we’re gonna need a safety plan here. So—what’s gonna work? My safety plans are ridiculous. I want you to take Chuckles when things get really bad.

Michelle: Like the candy?

Owen: The candy. Only when it’s serious.

Michelle: That sounds like a stupid safety plan.

Owen: It sounds like a stupid safety plan, but you’re laughing.

Michelle: Because it’s not pretending to be a serious safety plan. You’re presenting it with a wink and a nod. And yet you’re suggesting it—basically making a mockery of all other safety plans while you do it.

Owen: The thing that keeps you safe is mentalizing. How easy is it to kill yourself if you’re curious about what you’re doing?

And the suggestion to take a Chuckles as a treatment for acute suicidality is—

Michelle: Ridiculous.

Owen: But who made it?

Michelle: Someone who cares about you.

Owen: And suddenly, instead of thinking about killing yourself, you’re thinking about how funny the person who cares about you is. That they thought this would be helpful. And then you’re thinking about being cared for. Suddenly, someone held your mind in mind. And you felt understood.

The data backs it up. Mentalizing is basically a way they found to teach therapists how to be people.

The Language Has to Inspire Trust

Owen: The language matters because the language has to inspire trust in us to go with it. When I explain mentalization-based treatment, has anyone in the room heard this term before? No? Great. That means I can define it any way I want.

Michelle: It sounds smart, right?

Owen: Too many things we don’t know sound smart. And for some people, it sounds too smart. British accent equals— “Oh, I shouldn’t believe this, it’s different from my accent, and it’s probably something smart people do.” The exact same accent might have a totally opposite effect on you, depending on where you come from.

I’ve done MBT trainings where I do the introductory material, and the younger psychiatrists are like, “Wow, that’s great,”—and the older ones are like, “Eh.” Then a more senior colleague presents the same material, and the older psychiatrists are like, “This is great!” And the younger ones are lost.

I had assumed my introduction was way better. But it was only more relatable to some of the audience.

Michelle: So you want both.

Owen: Right. Having two different people teach it, even if it’s the same thing twice, is going to be different enough that it speaks to different people and reinforces the thing. This is why, in any given setting, you should have someone who’s culturally relevant to the audience and someone who’s not.

What Limits Us Is Simple

Michelle: How do you do it? How do you actually help people?

Owen: It’s about being curious. Making people feel comfortable enough to actually—

What limits us in psychiatry is really simple. The data we have is largely based on what people feel comfortable enough to actually tell us. And if we’ve built a system full of pretend mode—safety plans nobody believes in, handcuffs for panic attacks, hierarchies that ignore the people spending thousands of hours with patients—we are eroding the trust that is the only tool we have to get the real information we need.

Michelle: Most useful thing I was ever told was:

“if you need nursing care, you’re in a hospital. If you only need a doctor, you go to a doctor’s office. If you’re in a hospital, it’s because you need nurses around the clock.”

Most doctors don’t think that.

Owen: You don’t have to tell anybody that the nurses run the show. Except for the doctors. They don’t seem to get that.

Michelle: A good doctor, a good nurse—they’re both as important. They need each other. But not some power-hungry know-it-all—

Owen: Because knowing it all isn’t that helpful. Not in psychiatry. Not in medicine. I know a lot of things. I can tell most of my patients what to do from the get-go. But knowing what to do and getting someone to trust you enough to do it—those are two completely different problems.

Michelle: I guess that’s what it all is. It’s about being a good human.

Owen: Being a good human. Plus, when weird things happen, you should be able to recognize the difference.

All mentalization-based treatment is: some very, very thoughtful, smart people figured out that trust is really important, and that curiosity helps us get there faster and less dangerously than any other approach. And they figured out a way to turn that into a treatment.

And so I think it’s two steps. It’s being curious. And it’s getting back to being curious once we realize we’ve mucked it up.

writes on on Substack.

Owen Muir is an Anna Freud Centre MBT Supervisor and the Chief Medical Officer at Radial and Neurolief.

All mentalization-based treatment is: some very, very thoughtful, smart people figured out that trust is really important, and that curiosity helps us get there faster and less dangerously than any other approach. And they figured out a way to turn that into a treatment.

And so I think it’s two steps. It’s being curious. And it’s getting back to being curious once we realize we’ve mucked it up.
